title: Authentication: Token Pool
subtitle: How providers verify calls with short-lived tokens, and when a token pool is the better choice.
endNote: Next: direct routing, connecting providers peer to peer.

segments.text: Option one, direct query, asks the caller’s provider about every single call.
Option two, the token pool, is the alternative.
Before placing a call, the originating provider puts a short-lived token into a pool.
The receiving provider checks the pool to verify the call, instead of querying the originator directly.
A customer of Alpha Telecom calls 0161 496 0123. Before it sends the call, Alpha creates a token.
The token is unique, and it is valid for just thirty seconds.
Alpha records the call details against it: the caller, the number called and a call reference. The request is signed.
The token goes into the pool, and its ID travels with the call itself, inside the SIP invite.
Bravo Networks receives the call, with the token ID in the invite.
It looks the token up in the pool, with one simple GET request.
The details match the call in front of it: the same caller, the same number, and still in date. Verified.
If there is no matching token, or it has expired, the call fails verification.
Thirty seconds after it was created, the token expires, so a captured token is soon worthless.
A pool shared between providers needs governance.
A trusted body, such as a consortium of providers, runs the pool infrastructure.
It sets the rules: the token format, how long tokens last, and who may read and write them.
That creates accountability, while the data itself stays short-lived and spread across pools.
Token pools can scale better than direct queries, especially for small providers with high call volumes.
With direct query, a provider must run an authentication API that answers every incoming question.
With a token pool, a small provider simply writes to the pool, and reads from it.
The infrastructure is shared, so each provider carries less of the burden.
Several pool servers provide redundancy.
A provider can write each token to more than one pool at the same time.
So if one pool becomes unavailable, the others carry on, and the token can still be checked.
Verification stays available, even during a failure.
Token requests are signed with Ed25519 and carried over TLS 1.3, so tokens cannot be forged.
Only authenticated providers can reach a pool. Everyone else is shut out.
Rate limits stop anyone flooding the pool.
And every access is logged, giving a full audit trail.
Small providers benefit the most from token pools.
They need no authentication infrastructure of their own, and no service to answer incoming queries.
They just integrate with the pool API: one call to create a token, and one to check it. That is simpler, and cheaper, to build.
The two options can coexist.
Large providers may prefer direct query, for full control. Small providers may prefer the token pool, for simplicity.
The receiving provider can check both: the token pool first, then a direct query if there is no token.
And if neither is available, the call simply carries on over today’s network.
A shared pool adds governance, and a shared component, which direct query avoids.
In return, it can scale better for high-volume traffic.
The right choice depends on a provider’s size, its call volume, and whether it values control or simplicity.
Token pools could be run by industry groups, by regulators, or by commercial operators.
What matters is neutrality, and open access.
Any qualified provider should be able to take part, putting strong caller authentication within reach of every provider, large or small.
